q: A wine glass should be filled to roughly what level?
opts: Three-quarters full
The brim
The bowl's widest part
One-tenth full
exp: Leaving air above the wine is what makes swirling possible, so the widest part of the bowl is a ceiling rather than a target. A full glass cannot be assessed.

q: A forty-year-old red has thrown a heavy deposit. What is the decant chiefly achieving?
opts: To separate the wine from its sediment
To bring a cold cellar bottle up to serving temperature
To drive oxygen through it and open it up quickly
To remove tannin
exp: Old wine throws a deposit and is often fragile, so the decant is careful and served promptly. Hard aeration is the last thing it wants, and temperature is a side effect rather than the point.

q: A young Barolo is closed and grippy on opening. Why might you decant it?
opts: To aerate it and soften the tannin
To reduce its alcohol
To remove the heavy deposit a young Barolo throws
To chill it
exp: The opposite purpose from an old wine, and it may be poured vigorously and left to open for an hour or more. A wine this young has thrown little worth separating.

q: Why is a candle or light used beneath the neck when decanting?
opts: To warm the wine gently as it passes the flame
To watch the sediment approach the shoulder
Purely for the ceremony of the occasion
To inspect the cork for staining before pouring
exp: Any steady light works, and the flame is nowhere near the wine long enough to warm it. The point is the moment the deposit reaches the shoulder, when pouring stops.

q: Washing glassware with strongly scented detergent risks what?
opts: Residue that taints the aroma
Cracking the glass
Dulling the colour
Raising the serving temperature
exp: Glasses are best rinsed in very hot water and polished with a lint-free cloth. Detergent residue and cardboard smells both ruin a pour.

q: Where should the foil capsule be cut on a still wine bottle?
opts: Above the lip, so the foil stays neat
At the base of the neck
It is left in place and the cork drawn through
Below the lip of the bottle
exp: Cutting below the lip stops the wine touching foil on its way out. It is also tidier when the bottle is presented.

q: A sparkling wine bottle is opened by doing what?
opts: Holding the cork still and turning the bottle
Shaking then releasing quickly
Levering the cork with a corkscrew
Turning the cork briskly while the bottle is held still
exp: Turning the bottle gives control, and a thumb stays over the cork from the moment the cage is loosened. A sigh rather than a bang.

q: Why should a sparkling wine bottle never be pointed toward guests?
opts: Pointing the bottle at the table disturbs its sediment
A cork can leave under pressure and injure
It is a point of table etiquette rather than of safety
It warms the bottle
exp: The bottle holds around six atmospheres. Serious eye injuries happen every year, which makes this a safety rule rather than a nicety.

q: A standard pour of still wine in a restaurant is roughly what?
opts: A full glass
About 350 ml
About 150 ml
About 50 ml
exp: Five pours to a bottle at that size, about five ounces each, which is how by-the-glass pricing is built.

q: Twisting the bottle slightly as the pour finishes achieves what?
opts: It settles sediment
It aerates the wine
It is required by law
It stops drips down the bottle
exp: A small turn with a lifted neck stops the last drop running down the label. A serviette in the other hand covers what the turn misses.

q: If a cork breaks during extraction, what is the sound approach?
opts: Shake the bottle until the fragment works loose
Push the cork into the bottle immediately
Reinsert the worm at an angle
Discard the bottle and open another at once
exp: Come in shallow and draw out the remainder carefully. Pushing it in risks fragments and a wine that cannot be presented; failing that, decant through a fine strainer.

q: Why is the cork traditionally placed before the host?
opts: It proves the vintage
So the host may inspect it if they wish
It absorbs spills
It is used to reseal the bottle
exp: Largely ceremonial now, and smelling it tells you little a glass will not. A soaked or crumbling cork can hint at storage problems.

q: The bottle is presented to whom before opening?
opts: The eldest guest
Whoever is nearest
Nobody, it is opened at the sideboard
The person who ordered it
exp: The host confirms producer, wine and vintage before the foil is cut, which is the last moment an error can be caught cheaply.

q: After the host approves the wine, in what order are guests served?
opts: Nearest to the door first
Alphabetically
The host first, since they ordered and approved the wine
The other guests first, the host last
exp: The host tastes but is poured last. It is one of the clearest signals of trained service.

q: The host's initial taste is intended to establish what?
opts: That it is the correct temperature
That the price is acceptable
That the wine suits the host's own taste
That the wine is sound
exp: Soundness is the question, not preference. A wine disliked but not faulty is a conversation rather than an automatic replacement.

q: A guest declares a wine faulty and you disagree. What is the correct response?
opts: Replace it graciously
Refuse the complaint and charge for the bottle
Argue the point at the table
Insist the guest tastes it again
exp: Never litigate at the table. Check the bottle away from it afterwards; that tells you whether the case is worth raising with the supplier.
